paragraphs: AneuG-Flow addresses a data bottleneck in learning to predict blood flow around intracranial aneurysms. Detailed fluid simulations take time, while training faster neural predictors requires many examples pairing anatomy with flow measurements. The paper supplies synthetic aneurysm geometries together with simulated hemodynamics, supporting models that learn how vessel shape affects fluid behavior.

The dataset contains 14,000 steady-flow cases and 200 pulsatile-flow cases. Its geometry generator was trained on 109 real aneurysms at middle cerebral artery bifurcations, producing variations in aneurysm sacs and surrounding vessels. Simulations assume laminar flow and use meshes exceeding three million cells, with specified inlet velocity profiles and geometry-dependent flow splits at two outlets.

The released data include surface meshes, velocity, pressure, and wall shear stress, plus velocity and pressure gradients for transient cases. Results show substantial effects of geometry on flow patterns and forces. Tests with PointNet and graph U-Nets report a 4.67% relative L2 loss for normalized wall shear stress patterns, demonstrating a concrete prediction use for the dataset.
neurips-2025-aneug-flow-a-large-scale-sy.tldr: AneuG-Flow pairs diverse synthetic aneurysm shapes with detailed blood-flow simulations to support learning faster flow predictors.

paragraphs: AutoPartGen reconstructs 3D objects as collections of parts, giving the generation process an explicit compositional structure. It can start from an object image, two-dimensional masks identifying parts, or an existing 3D object. Across these input types, the goal is to produce corresponding three-dimensional components that fit together into a coherent whole.

The model builds on 3DShape2VecSet, a learned representation of 3D geometry. The authors observe that this representation supports composition particularly well. AutoPartGen predicts one part at a time, using both the supplied input and the parts it has already generated. It also decides when generation is complete, allowing the type and number of parts to emerge during reconstruction.

The resulting components can be assembled into objects or scenes without an additional optimization stage. This matters because producing plausible individual pieces is only useful if their combined geometry also makes sense. Evaluations examine both complete-object generation and part-level quality, with the authors reporting state-of-the-art performance in 3D part generation.
neurips-2025-autopartgen-autoregressive-.tldr: AutoPartGen builds coherent 3D objects one part at a time and automatically determines which parts, and how many, to generate.

paragraphs: This paper studies what happens when concepts inside a request or model representation conflict. The authors call this concept incongruence: the boundaries defining one concept clash with another, leaving expected behavior unclear or incorrectly specified. They examine a concrete case in role playing, where a character's death creates a temporal boundary for answering questions.

The study measures abstention rate, conditional accuracy, and answer rate to distinguish whether models answer and how accurately they do so. Models fail to abstain after the role's death and show lower accuracy than in a setting without role play. These findings expose problems in both respecting the role's temporal limits and retaining accurate answers.

Probing experiments identify unreliable representation of the death state across years and shifts in temporal representations induced by role playing. The authors use these insights to improve consistency in answering and abstaining. The contribution is an initial framework for analyzing conflicting concepts, with evidence that role instructions can alter internal representations in ways that affect observable behavior.
neurips-2025-concept-incongruence-an-exp.tldr: Conflicting temporal concepts in role play can disrupt language models' accuracy and abstention, partly through changes in their internal representations.

paragraphs: Detecting unusual nodes in a graph becomes difficult when information sharing blurs the very signals that distinguish them. The paper identifies two obstacles: graph neural networks can smooth away anomalies across connected nodes, and fraudulent nodes can disguise their features. CGADM approaches detection through repeated denoising and reconstruction, using diffusion to refine evidence about anomalous behavior.

Its central design is a diffusion process guided by an existing anomaly estimator. This pretrained estimator influences both the forward process and the reverse reconstruction process, so anomaly-related guidance is incorporated throughout the model. The approach connects prior predictions with iterative refinement rather than relying solely on a discriminative decision from node features.

For large graphs, CGADM also adjusts the number of reverse denoising steps according to confidence in the prior estimator. This makes computation adaptive to the available guidance. Benchmark experiments report state-of-the-art detection performance alongside significant computational advantages, suggesting that guided reconstruction can address detection quality and the cost of applying diffusion at graph scale.
neurips-2025-conditional-diffusion-anoma.tldr: CGADM uses anomaly-guided diffusion and confidence-dependent denoising to improve graph anomaly detection while reducing computational demands.

paragraphs: An agent exploring an open-ended environment may encounter different apparent cause-and-effect relationships as contexts change. The paper emphasizes that limited observations and shifts in policy or environment state can change the causal mechanisms the agent observes. A world model built around one fixed observed causal structure may therefore struggle to represent these experiences.

The proposed Meta-Causal Graph combines multiple causal subgraphs, each activated by a latent meta state. It represents both contextual causal relationships and the rules governing changes between them. The associated Causality-Seeking Agent tries to discover which meta states activate particular subgraphs and which causal relationships hold within each one.

Learning is driven by curiosity-based interventions and continued exploration, allowing the agent to refine its graph through experience. Experiments on synthetic tasks and robot arm manipulation show robust capture of changing causal dynamics and effective generalization to unseen contexts. These results support the usefulness of explicitly modeling context-dependent causal changes instead of treating every new observation as evidence about a single unchanging observed mechanism.
neurips-2025-curious-causality-seeking-a.tldr: A curiosity-driven agent learns context-dependent causal graphs and how they change, improving adaptation to unfamiliar situations in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Data attribution methods estimate how training examples influence a language model's outputs. Such estimates can guide data selection, help interpret model behavior, and inform assessments of data value. DATE-LM addresses the difficulty of evaluating these methods systematically by testing attribution through practical language-model applications within a shared benchmark.

The benchmark covers training data selection, toxicity and bias filtering, and factual attribution. These tasks ask different things of an attribution method, connecting its scores to distinct uses. DATE-LM is designed to support configurable, large-scale evaluations across tasks and model architectures, and includes a public leaderboard for comparing methods.

The authors' evaluation finds no method that performs best across every task. Attribution methods also involve trade-offs relative to simpler baselines, and their apparent quality changes with task-specific evaluation choices. The implication is that an attribution ranking needs to be interpreted in relation to its intended application. DATE-LM makes those comparisons more systematic while showing why one overall winner would obscure meaningful differences.
neurips-2025-date-lm-benchmarking-data-a.tldr: DATE-LM evaluates data attribution through three practical language-model tasks and finds that method quality depends strongly on the task and evaluation design.

paragraphs: Linear recurrent networks offer efficient sequence processing, but the structure of their state updates limits what they can represent. Simple diagonal transitions are fast, while richer transitions can mix information more expressively. DeltaProduct develops a controllable middle ground, building on DeltaNet's use of a diagonal-plus-rank-one state transition.

The starting insight is that DeltaNet's recurrence can be interpreted as one online gradient-descent step per token on an associative recall objective. DeltaProduct takes multiple such steps. This produces transitions formed from products of generalized Householder transformations, with a diagonal-plus-higher-rank structure. The number of transformations becomes a parameter for balancing expressive capacity against computational efficiency.

The paper theoretically characterizes state tracking under finite precision and how increasing the number of transformations improves that capability. Experiments report better state tracking and language modeling than DeltaNet, along with substantially improved length extrapolation. Together, these findings connect a specific change in recurrence structure to both a theoretical account of memory updates and observed improvements in sequence tasks.
neurips-2025-deltaproduct-improving-stat.tldr: DeltaProduct makes multiple structured updates per token to improve linear recurrent networks' state tracking, language modeling, and length extrapolation.

paragraphs: DISCO tackles the problem of steering a diffusion model toward user-specified conditions. The paper contrasts two established approaches: guidance using gradients from a differentiable target model, and guidance built into the diffusion model through joint training. These approaches introduce requirements on either the target model or the training and architecture.

DISCO turns conditional guidance into a discrete selection problem. It constructs a finite collection of noise vectors sampled from a Gaussian prior, then trains a prediction network to choose a code using the current diffusion state and the conditioning input. The selected vector takes the role of the continuous conditional correction used in other guidance approaches.

This design avoids requiring differentiable target models and the gradient computations associated with their guidance. The authors also describe it as training-efficient and less architecturally redundant. Empirical results show competitive control over outputs with substantially lower resource demands. The stated result is a practical alternative for conditional generation, with controllability maintained competitively rather than a claim of universally superior image generation.
neurips-2025-disco-discrete-noise-for-co.tldr: DISCO steers diffusion generation by selecting discrete noise codes, achieving competitive conditional control with reduced resource demands.

paragraphs: Dynam3D helps navigation agents connect language instructions with a persistent understanding of three-dimensional surroundings. Video-language models bring broad knowledge, but the paper identifies weaknesses in spatial geometry, long-term environmental memory, and adaptation to changes. Its solution is a structured 3D representation used as visual input for predicting navigation actions.

Given RGB-D images with camera poses, Dynam3D projects two-dimensional CLIP features into 3D space. It organizes the result into patches, instances, and zones, providing several levels of geometric and semantic description. An online, layer-wise update strategy locates and updates instances as the environment changes, supporting exploration and memory across larger spaces.

Training combines large-scale 3D-language pretraining with navigation-specific adaptation. The authors report state-of-the-art results on R2R-CE, REVERIE-CE, and NavRAG-CE under monocular settings. Experiments involving pre-exploration, lifelong memory, and a real robot also support practical deployment. The contribution links navigation decisions to an environment representation that can accumulate knowledge while remaining responsive to changes.
neurips-2025-dynam3d-dynamic-layered-3d-.tldr: Dynam3D gives language-guided navigation agents an updateable, hierarchical 3D representation that supports spatial understanding and long-term memory.

paragraphs: Graph networks that pass messages through local neighborhoods face two distinct difficulties: node representations can become too similar, and information from distant nodes can become compressed or weakened. Dropout-style methods have helped with the first problem, called over-smoothing. This paper investigates whether they also support the long-range interactions threatened by over-squashing.

The authors analyze several edge-dropping and related methods, deriving results showing that DropEdge variants reduce sensitivity between distant nodes. They introduce DropSens to control how much information edge removal loses. Developed around graph convolutional network message passing, it preserves greater sensitivity to distant nodes while removing the same number of edges.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world long-range tasks confirm the predicted weaknesses of existing edge- and feature-dropping methods. DropSens combined with GCN consistently beats graph rewiring methods targeting over-squashing in the reported experiments. The finding motivates evaluating dropout by which information it removes, since reducing over-smoothing alone does not establish suitability for learning distant relationships.
neurips-2025-effects-of-dropout-on-perfo.tldr: Common graph dropout methods can weaken distant interactions; DropSens controls information loss to improve long-range learning with GCN.

paragraphs: Federated prompt learning adapts pretrained models by learning prompt embeddings across a federated setting. Many algorithms have appeared, but inconsistent protocols and narrow evaluations make their strengths hard to compare. FLiP provides a standardized benchmark intended to clarify which methods suit different scenarios and how much specialized federated designs contribute.

The benchmark evaluates 13 centralized and federated prompt-learning methods across three federated protocols, 12 open datasets, and six evaluation scenarios. Including centralized methods adapted to the setting is an important part of the comparison: it tests whether existing prompt-learning approaches remain competitive alongside algorithms designed specifically for federation.

The results show strong prompt-learning generalization within and outside the training distribution while using few resources. They also show that no single method works best across the diverse scenarios, and that adapted centralized methods can be competitive. FLiP therefore supports scenario-specific choices and a clearer interpretation of algorithm effectiveness, with released benchmarks and code enabling further evaluation under shared conditions.
neurips-2025-flip-towards-comprehensive-.tldr: FLiP standardizes federated prompt-learning evaluation and finds strong efficiency and generalization, but no universally best method.

paragraphs: GradMetaNet is a neural architecture designed to process the gradients of other neural networks. Gradients contain information useful for optimization, model editing, and analysis, but learning directly from them requires handling their structure. The paper argues that architectures without a gradient-specific design restrict what these learned algorithms can do.

Three principles guide the design. Equivariance preserves the symmetries created by permuting neurons, so processing remains consistent with those rearrangements. Sets of gradients from multiple data points provide information about loss curvature. Rank-one decomposition supplies an efficient representation of gradients. GradMetaNet combines these principles through simple equivariant building blocks.

The authors prove universality results and show that some natural functions of gradients can be approximated by GradMetaNet but not by previous approaches. They also demonstrate applications to multilayer perceptrons and transformers, including learned optimization, implicit neural representation editing, and curvature estimation. The contribution combines a stronger account of representational capability with evidence that gradient-aware structure is useful across several tasks.
neurips-2025-gradmetanet-an-equivariant-.tldr: GradMetaNet processes gradients using neuron symmetries, multiple examples, and efficient decompositions to support learned optimization, editing, and analysis.

paragraphs: HBLLM compresses the weights of an already trained language model toward one-bit storage while aiming to retain model quality. At such low precision, the way weights are represented and grouped becomes central to preserving information. The method uses a Haar wavelet transform to separate frequency components and improve the expressive capacity of the quantized representation.

Its grouping strategy accounts for structure in two ways. Within rows, it uses frequency-aware groups with multiple parameters. Across columns, it uses L2 norms to select salient weights. For weights treated as non-salient, groups within each frequency band share a mean, reducing the storage required for supporting information.

Experiments on OPT and LLaMA models report state-of-the-art one-bit quantization performance. One stated result is a perplexity of 6.71 for LLaMA2-13B with average weight storage of 1.08 bits. That average captures the method's storage beyond the one-bit label. The results support combining frequency decomposition and selective parameter allocation to improve fidelity while keeping overhead small.
neurips-2025-hbllm-wavelet-enhanced-high.tldr: HBLLM combines wavelet decomposition and structure-aware grouping to preserve language-model quality at approximately one bit per weight.

paragraphs: Editing or moving an object in a reconstructed 3D scene can leave geometry that needs repair. Existing inpainting approaches rely on expensive optimization, making this repair difficult to integrate into interactive experiences. InstaInpaint targets the delay with a feed-forward framework that produces a repaired 3D scene from a two-dimensional inpainting proposal.

The method uses a custom large reconstruction model trained through self-supervised masked fine-tuning on a large-scale dataset. This training strategy enables the reconstruction model to handle the inpainting task. The authors also investigate design choices affecting generalization, agreement of textures, and geometric correctness, connecting fast prediction to the requirements of coherent scene repair.

InstaInpaint reports an inpainting time of 0.4 seconds and a thousandfold speed-up over prior methods while maintaining state-of-the-art performance on two standard benchmarks. The paper also demonstrates generalization to object insertion and repairing multiple regions. These findings support the use of learned direct reconstruction for scene editing where a lengthy optimization stage would obstruct interaction.
neurips-2025-instainpaint-instant-3d-sce.tldr: InstaInpaint converts a 2D inpainting proposal into a repaired 3D scene in 0.4 seconds using a trained reconstruction model.

paragraphs: Membership inference asks whether a particular example was part of a model's training data. It is useful for auditing privacy risks when training collections may contain sensitive information. Existing attacks on large vision-language models often assume access to full prediction scores, although deployed systems may expose only their highest-ranked prediction.

LOMIA studies this more restrictive setting and proposes three attack methods using only top-one predictions. The shared intuition is that memorized training examples are more likely to produce outputs with stronger semantic alignment and lower perplexity. These observable output characteristics provide signals for distinguishing potential training members without direct access to the model's full logits.

Experiments cover three widely used open-source vision-language models and GPT-4o. The framework outperforms existing label-only adaptations and is competitive with state-of-the-art attacks that use logits across the reported metrics. The findings show that restricting access to prediction scores can still leave useful membership signals, making label-only auditing relevant to privacy assessment in deployed multimodal systems.
neurips-2025-lomia-label-only-membership.tldr: LOMIA infers potential training-data membership from vision-language models' top predictions without requiring their full prediction scores.

paragraphs: Cooperative agents can improve their decisions by exchanging messages, but real communication is often lossy. The paper addresses the difficulty of learning coordinated behavior when message quality varies across scenarios. It identifies scalability and robustness as obstacles for existing communication-based multi-agent reinforcement learning in complex, changing environments.

The approach begins with a generalized model of communication constraints that characterizes conditions across different scenarios. This model becomes a learning prior for distinguishing lossy messages from lossless ones in a particular setting. The framework therefore incorporates knowledge about communication conditions into the learning process, rather than treating all received information as equivalent.

A dual mutual-information estimator is used to separate how the two message categories affect distributed decisions. Their influence is then quantified within the global reward, connecting communication effects to cooperative policy learning. Experiments across several communication-constrained benchmarks validate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution is a framework for making message reliability an explicit part of how agents learn to cooperate under constrained communication.
neurips-2025-multi-agent-reinforcement-l.tldr: This framework incorporates communication constraints and message reliability into multi-agent reinforcement learning to support cooperation under lossy communication.

paragraphs: This paper studies recurrent networks for estimating conditional quantiles, which describe different positions within an outcome distribution given the available information. It considers both ordinary and sparse recurrent neural networks with ReLU activations. The central question is how accurately these models can estimate a structured quantile function from dependent observations.

The theoretical result relies on specific assumptions. The conditional quantile function follows a compositional hierarchical interaction model, and the observations come from a stationary process with exponentially decaying beta-mixing dependence. Under these conditions and appropriately chosen architectures, the estimators achieve the optimal nonparametric convergence rate up to a logarithmic factor.

To establish that rate, the authors derive sharp bounds on how well the recurrent architectures approximate functions in the assumed class. Their analysis uses connections to sparse feedforward networks. Numerical experiments and a study of the Dow Jones Industrial Average support the theoretical findings. The contribution is a conditional statistical guarantee linking recurrent architecture design, function structure, and dependence in sequential data.
neurips-2025-nonparametric-quantile-regr.tldr: Properly designed ReLU recurrent networks attain near-optimal quantile-estimation rates under stated structural and time-dependence assumptions.

paragraphs: ORBIT aims to make recommendation research easier to compare and more representative of realistic behavior. Existing datasets and inconsistent evaluation settings can produce ambiguous conclusions about model quality. The benchmark standardizes public dataset splits and evaluation settings, giving its public leaderboard a reproducible basis for comparing recommendation approaches.

It also introduces ClueWeb-Reco, a webpage recommendation task based on browsing sequences involving 87 million public, high-quality webpages. This synthetic dataset is derived from real browsing data described as user-consented and privacy-guaranteed. It serves as the leaderboard's hidden test, providing a separate challenge for evaluating how recommendation models generalize.

The study evaluates 12 representative models on the public benchmark and introduces a prompted language-model baseline for the hidden task. Public results show general improvements with varying individual performance, while hidden-test results expose weaknesses in large-scale webpage recommendation. They also suggest potential benefits from integrating language models. Together, the two evaluation components connect reproducible comparisons with a demanding test of generalization.
neurips-2025-orbit-open-recommendation-b.tldr: ORBIT combines reproducible recommendation benchmarks with a hidden webpage recommendation test that reveals generalization challenges.

paragraphs: Comparing models at a few isolated training scales can give a misleading picture of which approach is preferable. This paper uses scaling laws to compare language-vision models and datasets across a broad, shared compute range. It derives those laws from dense measurements spanning model sizes and numbers of training samples seen.

The study compares CLIP's contrastive objective with MaMMUT's combination of contrastive learning and caption generation, using DataComp-1.4B, Re-LAION-1.4B, and DFN-1.4B. Predictions are checked on held-out measurements. The comparisons provide evidence that MaMMUT improves more strongly with scale and uses samples more efficiently, while DFN-1.4B performs better than the other evaluated datasets.

Classification, retrieval, and segmentation show consistent scaling trends. The authors also show that constant learning-rate schedules can reduce the cost of deriving comparison laws. Released models include openMaMMUT-L/14, achieving 80.3% zero-shot ImageNet-1k accuracy after seeing 12.8 billion DataComp samples. The broader contribution is a framework for comparisons that account explicitly for scale and compute.
neurips-2025-scaling-laws-for-robust-com.tldr: Scaling laws enable model and dataset comparisons across compute budgets, with evidence favoring MaMMUT's scaling and DFN-1.4B in the studied settings.

paragraphs: Shallow Diffuse embeds watermarks in diffusion-generated images so that their artificial origin can be identified. The method aims for watermarks that remain detectable without becoming visible in the image. Its central concern is separating watermark insertion from image generation, since existing approaches incorporate watermarking throughout the diffusion sampling process.

The technique uses a low-dimensional subspace present in generation. It places a substantial portion of the watermark in that subspace's null space, separating much of the watermark signal from the generation process. This geometric construction is the mechanism for decoupling the two operations while retaining a signal that can be detected.

Theoretical and empirical analyses show improved generation consistency and watermark detectability from this separation. Further experiments report better consistency than existing watermarking methods. The contribution therefore links the placement of a watermark to how strongly it interacts with image generation, providing evidence that exploiting the process's subspace structure can support both consistent outputs and identifiable watermarks.
neurips-2025-shallow-diffuse-robust-and-.tldr: Shallow Diffuse separates watermark signals from diffusion image generation through subspace structure, improving consistency and detectability.

paragraphs: Latent stochastic differential equations describe evolving systems whose internal states are only indirectly observed. Recovering a distribution over their hidden state trajectories is typically intractable, so researchers use approximations. SING addresses slow convergence and numerical instability in variational inference methods used for this task.

The method uses natural gradients to account for the geometry of the model and its approximate posterior distribution. It also approximates otherwise intractable integrals and parallelizes calculations across time. The paper provides theoretical guarantees of approximate optimization of the continuous-time objective, connecting the computational procedure to the inference problem it is intended to solve.

Experiments show that improved state inference also supports more accurate estimation of nonlinear drift functions, which describe the system's underlying dynamics. SING outperforms prior methods on state inference and drift estimation across multiple datasets, including neural dynamics in freely behaving animals. The findings support its potential for learning complex dynamics, particularly with limited prior knowledge and structures that resist convenient inference formulas.
neurips-2025-sing-sde-inference-via-natu.tldr: SING uses natural-gradient variational inference to improve hidden-state recovery and dynamics estimation in stochastic differential equation models.

paragraphs: This paper asks where learned information appears in transformer weight matrices when they are decomposed into singular values and associated directions. Large singular values usually receive attention, but the authors also examine the smallest ones. Random matrix theory supplies a zero-information reference, with deviations treated as evidence of learned structure.

Both ends of the spectrum show pronounced departures from that reference. The associated directions overlap substantially with directions in activation covariance wherever those departures occur. This suggests that small singular values can accompany meaningful data directions, so their small magnitude alone does not establish that they are unimportant.

Removing singular values that depart from the random reference increases perplexity much more than removing values from the bulk. After fine-tuning, the smallest tenth can be the spectrum's third most influential portion. A linear random-matrix model helps explain how this can happen. The findings inform compression and pruning by showing why decisions based only on singular-value magnitude may discard learned information.
neurips-2025-small-singular-values-matte.tldr: Small singular values can encode important learned information in transformers, making magnitude alone an unreliable guide for compression.

paragraphs: SPARTAN learns how objects interact so that a world model can predict their future states and adapt when dynamics change. The paper identifies reliable discovery of local interaction structure as a challenge in complex environments. It proposes sparsity as a key ingredient for making those learned relationships selective and interpretable.

The model represents objects with separate tokens and regularizes attention to favor sparse connections between them. The resulting interaction graph depends on context, allowing relevant relationships to change with the scene. An extension handles sparse interventions on environmental dynamics even when the affected targets are unknown, supporting adaptation to localized changes.

Evaluations compare SPARTAN with state-of-the-art object-centric world models in observation-based environments. The reported results show learned local causal graphs that reflect underlying object interactions, improved adaptation from few examples after dynamics changes, and greater robustness to distractors. These findings support sparse attention as a useful structural bias for discovering interactions and making world models easier to adapt.
neurips-2025-spartan-a-sparse-transforme.tldr: SPARTAN learns sparse, context-dependent object interactions to improve world-model prediction, adaptation to changed dynamics, and distractor robustness.

paragraphs: SRPO aims to make multimodal language models better at examining and correcting their own reasoning. The paper argues that existing reflection methods often produce feedback that is too simplistic to help with complex problems. Its approach explicitly trains reflection alongside reasoning, then rewards useful reflection during reinforcement learning.

The first stage builds a reflection-focused dataset with guidance from a more advanced multimodal model. That model generates reflections based on initial responses, giving the policy model examples of both reasoning and reviewing its reasoning. The second stage introduces a reward within Group Relative Policy Optimization that encourages concise, meaningful reflection while discouraging redundancy.

Experiments use Qwen-2.5-VL models with 7 billion and 32 billion parameters across MathVista, MathVision, Mathverse, and MMMU-Pro. The authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art models in reasoning accuracy and reflection quality. The results support treating reflection as a learned and rewarded capability, with the quality of feedback central to the framework rather than simply generating more reflective text.
neurips-2025-srpo-enhancing-multimodal-l.tldr: SRPO combines reflection-focused training data with reinforcement-learning rewards for concise, useful self-reflection to improve multimodal reasoning.

paragraphs: This work combines a portable demonstration-collection device with a learning method for precise robotic manipulation. Handheld grippers are convenient for gathering human demonstrations, but many lack touch sensing. The proposed lightweight gripper records synchronized visual and tactile information in varied real-world settings, capturing both what an interaction looks like and its contact feedback.

The learning framework combines these two signal types while preserving their distinct characteristics. Its learned representations consistently emphasize contact regions relevant to physical interaction, making their focus interpretable. Those representations are then used to learn manipulation policies, with the authors reporting more efficient and effective learning from multimodal feedback.

Validation includes test tube insertion and fluid transfer using a pipette, tasks that require fine control of physical interactions. The results show improved accuracy and robustness under external disturbances. The contribution connects portable data collection to a representation that highlights contact, demonstrating how tactile information can support precise action when integrated with vision.
neurips-2025-touch-in-the-wild-learning-.tldr: A portable vision-and-touch gripper and contact-focused representation learning improve precise robotic manipulation and robustness to disturbances.
